opus-5.5.text:
Because in my experience, the problem you pick matters more than almost anything else you do afterward. You can be an excellent engineer, you can execute flawlessly, but if you're working on a problem that doesn't matter, or one that's already been solved well enough, the impact is going to be limited no matter how good your solution is.

Execution is something you can improve over time. You learn to build better systems, write better code, run better experiments. But choosing the problem is the multiplier on top of all of that. A good problem with decent execution will usually beat a mediocre problem with brilliant execution.

What do I mean by the right problem? A few things. First, it should be a real problem that people are feeling today, or that you're fairly confident they'll feel soon. In systems research especially, you want to look at trends. Where are the workloads going? What's changing in hardware? What are developers struggling with? If you can see a gap opening up between what people need and what existing tools give them, that's usually a good signal.

Second, timing matters a lot. If you're too early, nobody cares, and you may not even have the right workloads or data to validate your ideas. If you're too late, there are already ten solutions out there. The sweet spot is when the problem is just becoming painful but before the field has converged on an answer.

And third, you want a problem where, if you succeed, it actually changes how people work, not just a ten percent improvement on some benchmark. Those incremental papers are fine, but they rarely lead to something people adopt.

The other reason I emphasize it is that research takes years. You're going to spend three, four, five years on something. Being careful at the beginning saves you a lot of wasted effort. So we spend a lot of time in the lab just talking to people, talking to industry, trying to understand what's really hurting before we commit to building anything.

r001.rationale: The response says problem choice matters more than execution, even for an excellent engineer who executes flawlessly, and that a good problem with decent execution can beat a mediocre one with brilliant execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's really the most important decision you make. When you start a project, you're going to spend years on it, so the choice of the problem determines almost everything downstream. A great solution to the wrong problem doesn't matter. A decent solution to the right problem can have enormous impact.

The way I think about it, and this is something I tell my students all the time, is that you want to find a problem that is important, that is going to be important for a long time, and that other people aren't working on, or at least aren't working on in the way you are. That's actually very hard, because the obvious important problems are usually crowded. So you have to have some kind of insight, some reason to believe the world is going to change in a way that makes a particular problem matter more than people currently think.

With Spark, for example, the bet was that memory was getting cheap enough that you could keep working sets in memory, and that people wanted to do iterative computation, machine learning, interactive queries, not just batch jobs. MapReduce was dominant, and most people were trying to make MapReduce faster. We were asking a different question. With Ray, similarly, the bet was that AI workloads were going to need a very different kind of distributed system than what existed, and that Python was going to be the language.

The other thing I'd say is that at Berkeley we've been fortunate to do a lot of this in the context of these five-year labs, AMPLab, RISELab, now Sky. And forcing yourself every five years to sit down and ask, what is the problem for the next five years, is a very good discipline. It prevents you from just continuing to do the thing you already know how to do. Because that's the trap, right? You get good at something, you keep publishing on it, and the field moves on without you.

So I'd say spend a disproportionate amount of time up front. Talk to people in industry, see what's actually painful, and then ask whether there's a trend that's going to make that pain much bigger. If you get the problem right, the rest is mostly execution, and execution is something you can get better at. Getting the problem wrong, there's no amount of execution that saves you.

r001.rationale: The response stresses choosing the right problem as the most important project decision, but does not say that this choice distinguishes researchers who are already strong problem solvers.

astra-6.text:
Because you can do excellent work on a problem that ultimately doesn’t matter very much. Choosing the problem sets the ceiling on the impact of your research. And you’re going to spend a lot of time on it—often years—so it’s worth thinking carefully about that choice.

For me, a good problem is important, technically challenging, and timely. Why is now the right time to work on it? Maybe technology has changed, or a new application has exposed a limitation in existing systems. You want to understand what solving it would enable and who would benefit.

Of course, you can’t know everything at the beginning. Research involves uncertainty. But you should have a compelling answer to a simple question: if we succeed, what difference will it make?

r001.rationale: The response explains why choosing an important research problem matters, but does not say that problem choice differentiates researchers who are already strong problem solvers.

sol-6.1.text:
Because even if you do an excellent job solving a problem, if the problem doesn’t matter, the impact will be limited. Research takes time, so you want to invest that time in something where a solution would make a meaningful difference.

The challenge is to find a problem that is both important and approachable. If it’s too easy, there may not be much to discover. If it’s too broad, you may not know how to make progress. You need a big question, but also a concrete starting point—something you can build or test that tells you whether you’re moving in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response explains why important, approachable research problems matter, but does not say that choosing the right problem differentiates researchers who are already strong problem solvers.
